strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored problem: evaluating whether embodied agents can use prior interactions to resolve personalized references rather than merely follow explicit commands.

For single-memory tasks, pairing acquisition and utilization episodes with the same scene and goal is a sensible diagnostic design. Same-category distractors and the object-semantics/user-pattern taxonomy provide interpretable evaluation axes.

The empirical study covers six proprietary and open-weight LLMs of different sizes and reports task success, partial completion, planning cost, top-k sensitivity, memory representation, ambiguous instructions, and qualitative errors.
The manuscript is clear and well organized, documents the simulated agent architecture, and appropriately acknowledges limitations involving simulation, oracle skills, perception, and privacy.
weaknesses: The headline joint-memory result does not isolate multi-memory utilization. Joint tasks concatenate two episodes and therefore contain more predicates and a longer planning horizon, but performance is compared against individual acquisition episodes rather than an equally long explicit joint-task control. Increased steps and lower binary success can arise from ordinary error compounding; consequently, the reported 30.5-point GPT-4o drop cannot be causally attributed to integrating multiple memories.

Even the single-memory evaluation does not isolate goal interpretation as strongly as claimed: end-to-end success mixes memory use, instruction grounding, high-level planning, and execution. The paper should directly evaluate reconstructed object-location goals and then measure execution conditional on a correct goal.

Utilization repeats the exact scene and underlying goal, while episodic memory contains complete ReAct trajectories with object handles, actions, and observations. Agents can therefore replay a prior solution rather than infer transferable personalized semantics. The advantage of full trajectories in Table 2 may reflect this solution leakage; changed-state, counterfactual-goal, or cross-scene tests are missing.

The benchmark models a narrow, synthetic form of personalization. GPT-4o invents one-shot associations and labels a single demonstrated configuration as a user routine. It does not evaluate repeated evidence, evolving or conflicting preferences, multiple users, temporal effects, or natural instructions from real users. Same-scene retrieval, only 12 scenes, and just 36 joint episodes further limit generality.

Dataset construction and validation are circular: GPT-4o generates captions, personalized knowledge, and instructions, and is also used for feasibility filtering and gold trajectories. Excluding all 31 episodes that GPT-4o failed five times can favor that model and remove valid difficult examples. There is no systematic independent human audit, inter-annotator agreement, or naturalness/ambiguity study over the retained data.

The evaluation uses one retrieval pipeline and forcibly inserts the relevant memory into the top-5 context. There are no competitive memory-system baselines such as structured fact extraction, reranking, dedicated memory architectures, or an oracle personalized-fact representation, so the experiments mainly rank backbone LLMs rather than establish how memory methods perform on the benchmark.

The main results lack confidence intervals, significance tests, and repeated runs; this is especially problematic for the 36 joint tasks and 12 examples per joint knowledge combination. Reproducibility is also limited by missing exact API snapshots, seeds, released episode identifiers/data/code location, and complete few-shot prompt exemplars. These validity and reproducibility gaps are too substantial for a top-tier benchmark paper.
